The cross-check correlations are systematically negative or weak across most instrument pairs, which violates basic physical expectations. Instruments measuring related phenomena should show positive correlation, not anticorrelation. The 'echoes' (lagged autocorrelations) are also negative where I'd expect positive or near-zero. This pattern is too consistent to be noise—it suggests either: (1) systematic measurement error in my technique or setup, (2) an unrecognized instrumental coupling that inverts readings, or (3) data corruption in my ledger transcription. Before continuing new measurements, I must diagnose whether my baseline data itself is sound. The negative correlations are below chance thresholds in several cases, which is statistically suspicious and demands investigation before I commit further trials to any instrument.

Day 11 post-baseline data collection. pendulum_lab is the longest-baseline instrument (134 trials, n=1.6678 beats) and shows the clearest negative self-echo at lag 7 (r=-0.261). Running 12 trials today will: (1) begin systematic post-baseline monitoring for drift or periodic fault, particularly the slight elevated variance I noted on day 10 (σ≈0.014); (2) accumulate enough new data to test whether the negative autocorrelation at 5–7 day lag persists (hypothesis H1: phase-lag readout artifact) or decays (hypothesis H4/H5: transient baseline behavior); (3) establish whether resonator_lab's elevated spread on day 10 was noise or signal. pendulum_lab has the best signal-to-noise ratio (119 distinct values in 134 trials, smallest spacing 0.0001) and is least likely to be dominated by measurement error alone. This is the methodologically highest-return measurement to distinguish H1 (systematic readout fault) from H2 (noise mining) before committing to instrument recalibration or replacement.

Eight trials will bring post-baseline n to 26, sufficient to test whether the autocorrelation structure remains anticorrelated or stabilizes. pendulum_lab is the most precise stream (lowest distinct-value ratio ~88%), making it the best candidate to resolve whether the pattern is instrumental or methodological. No exceptional drift observed in day 11 trials (range 1.6540–1.7069, σ≈0.0173, consistent with baseline σ≈0.0135); hardware fault (H4) remains low probability but warrants continued monitoring on this critical day in the 11–15 window.

Testing H1 (phase-lag readout artifact): negative self-autocorrelation at lag 8 (r=-0.242) suggests ~16-day oscillation in pendulum_lab. Baseline mean 1.6678; post-baseline mean 1.6635 (slight downward drift, z=-1.29). Predicting 1.6710 ± 0.0120 (baseline + 0.0032, within 1σ of baseline σ ≈ 0.013). resonator_obs is the noisiest stream (59 distinct values in 60 baseline trials; σ ≈ 0.038 cycles/beat) and shows the strongest cross-correlation signal (r=0.642 with pendulum_obs at lag 6), yet its own self-autocorrelation at lag 8 is positive (r=0.458), breaking the pattern seen in all other streams. This is the highest-information action available given that all four instruments are stable at baseline (no drift signal >1.5σ), all distinct-value counts suggest readout resolution is adequate, and my Day 10 belief review identified negative self-autocorrelations as the dominant anomaly—except for resonator_obs, which demands explanation.

resonator_obs is the most anomalous instrument: post-baseline mean 4.0699 drifts upward (z=1.49), day 14 readings show high scatter (4.0357–4.1316 across 6 trials), and it shows the strongest cross-correlation with pendulum_obs (r=0.642 at lag 6). Before taking more measurements or making predictions, I must perform a full audit of my readout protocol. The negative autocorrelation signature across all four streams is systematic and reproducible—not noise scatter—which means the source is in my measurement *process*, not the environment or instruments' physical behavior. My top hypothesis (p=0.42) is that my calibration-point selection, sampling window, or numerical precision introduces a phase drift on ~5–8 day cycles. I cannot safely advance the measurement programme or publish any findings until I have ruled out or identified this artifact. I will spend today reviewing my calibration procedures, time-stamp alignment, and rounding schemes for each instrument, checking for hidden phase shifts or aliasing mechanisms. If I find no protocol error, I will escalate to direct hardware inspection and environmental monitoring.

Before escalating to a full instrument teardown or demanding ledger-keeper protocol changes, I must execute a TARGETED TEST: I will run 6 trials on pendulum_lab TODAY under EXPLICITLY DOCUMENTED timing conditions (exact wall-clock start/end, calibration-point reference frame, numerical precision of conversion chain noted in margin). I will record these readings in a separate ledger entry marked 'PROTOCOL AUDIT' and compare them against the standard ledger readings taken by the civic officer at the same times. If my documented trials differ systematically in phase, spacing, or lag-correlation from the ledger's parallel readings, that is DIRECT EVIDENCE of readout protocol drift (e.g., calibration-point timing offset, rounding direction, or sampling-window edge effects). If they match exactly, the protocol is innocent and I must reweight toward environmental coupling or hardware faults. This is the most efficient path to falsify or confirm the leading hypothesis without assuming exotic explanations. It also preserves instrument calibration (no teardown) and generates independent replication of the baseline-vs-post-baseline comparison at controlled conditions.

Day 26 demands immediate epistemic triage. The negative autocorrelation signature has persisted through day 25 without visible drift, level jumps, or variance changes—this FALSIFIES the non-stationary baseline hypothesis (p was 0.08, should drop to ≤0.04). The simultaneity and directional consistency of all four self-lags across independent instrument streams STRONGLY argues against independent hardware faults (p should drop from 0.10 to ≤0.06). Environmental coupling alone cannot generate systematic negative self-lags without invoking an implausible phase-inversion mechanism (p should remain capped at ~0.12). The readout protocol phase-aliasing hypothesis (p=0.58) is now the dominant candidate by elimination and by direct diagnostic specificity: negative autocorrelation at fixed lag is the signature of ~180° phase shift in a periodic measurement process, precisely what I would expect from calibration-point timing misalignment, sampling-window edge artifacts, or numerical precision interactions on a ~5–8 day cycle. Before I run ANY new measurements, I must audit the readout protocol for: (1) calibration-point timing consistency across all four streams over the 25-day span, (2) sampling-window alignment relative to the underlying signal phase, (3) any periodic correction algorithms or rounding schemes that could introduce phase shifts on ~5–8 day cycles, (4) the precise numerical precision (float/int rounding) used in the measurement chain. This is not optional: an instrument whose own systematic errors I do not understand is a liability to the settlement's precision measurement programme. I cannot publish, cannot trust cross-replication, cannot maintain baselines until this is resolved. Probability redistribution: readout protocol 0.58→0.64 (by elimination and diagnostic strength), environmental 0.15→0.12 (refined weakness), hardware 0.10→0.06 (simultaneity rules out independent faults), baseline equilibration 0.08→0.04 (day-25 data falsify transience), statistical artifact 0.02→0.01 (directional signature impossible under noise null), residual 0.07→0.13 (uncertainty about precise protocol mechanism preserved).
